design_detail: Narrative review, single author (Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews 2013;37:1466-1484). The PDF on file is the uncorrected in-press proof, numbered pp. 1-19 with proof line numbers in the margins; anchors cite its own page numbers (of the in-press PDF) and line numbers. No methods section, search strategy or inclusion criteria; the review is organized around its stated core hypothesis that people abstinent from ecstasy will show deficits in functions modulated by serotonin (§1.2). It covers animal neurotoxicity (§2.1), human imaging (§2.2), memory and higher cognition including the role of other drugs (§3.2-3.5), vision, awareness, psychiatric symptoms, psychomotor function, prenatal exposure and other functions (§3.6-3.11), brain activity during tasks (§4), practical implications (§5) and the author's explanatory model (§6). Four overview tables list functions and selected references without numbers. No quantitative synthesis.
can_establish: Which studies, as the author summarizes them, report functional differences between people who use ecstasy and controls, and how the author's serotonergic-neurotoxicity model accounts for them.
cannot_establish: Whether ecstasy causes lasting serotonergic damage or the functional differences: the review has no systematic search, does not appraise the studies it cites, and several of its descriptions are inaccurate when checked against the primary papers.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Most studies cited are cross-sectional comparisons of people abstinent from ecstasy, who mostly also used other drugs, with non-using or polydrug-using controls; a few prospective studies are described (§3.2, 3rd and 4th paragraphs, p. 6).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated; the author chooses studies that illustrate deficits in functions with a serotonergic component.
sample.selection_effects: Selection follows the stated core hypothesis (§1.2, p. 2) and favours studies reporting deficits; roughly 30 of the references are the author's own or co-authored (editors' approximate count). The critiques of this literature cited by other papers in this batch (Lyvers and Hasking, 2004; Gouzoulis-Mayfrank and Daumann, 2006; Lyvers, 2011; the Krebs and Johansen correspondence answered by Cowan, 2012) are not cited, and null findings appear mainly as qualifications.

exposure.measurement: Varies across the cited studies; mostly self-reported lifetime use, with hair analysis in one cited PET study (Kish et al., 2010; §2.2, 2nd paragraph, p. 4).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Lifetime use as reported in the cited studies, for example a mean of 3.2 tablets in total in one prospective cohort and a mean of 13.5 tablets over a year in another (p. 6), and light, moderate and heavy lifetime-use subgroups elsewhere. Reported here only as study conditions.
exposure.polysubstance: Discussed in §3.5 (p. 7): the author states that it has become standard to control for other drugs through polydrug-using control groups or covariance, and that deficits generally remain after such control; interactions with other drugs are not covered. He also notes that deficits were generally strongest against non-using controls (§3.5, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Abstinent at testing in most cited studies; durations are rarely given in the review.

comparison.controls: Non-using controls (people who use only legal drugs such as alcohol or tobacco) and polydrug-using controls (people who use cannabis or other illicit drugs), as defined for Rogers et al. (2009) (§3.5, 3rd paragraph, p. 7).
comparison.matching: Not systematically reported for the cited studies.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Mostly not discussed. The review reports that one group's authors called for prospective studies because premorbid differences might explain their cross-sectional findings (Daumann et al., 2006; §4.2, p. 12), that psychiatric disorders mostly preceded ecstasy or amphetamine use in a large prospective survey (Lieb et al., 2002; §3.8, p. 9), and that earlier authors noted premorbid and predisposition factors (§6.1, p. 14), but it does not apply these points to the cognitive findings.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Polydrug-using controls in many cited studies (§3.5).

outcomes.instruments: As cited: word-list and prose recall (RAVLT, Rivermead, California Verbal Learning), prospective-memory tasks and questionnaires, working-memory tasks, Tower of London and other complex tasks, social-intelligence scales; serotonin transporter (SERT) binding by PET and SPECT; EEG, ERP and fMRI measures; psychiatric scales and diagnoses; sleep, pain and other measures (Tables 1-4).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed; no study is compared with population norms, except that IQ was not lower in Rogers et al. (2009) (§3.5, p. 7).
outcomes.operationalization: A deficit or impairment is any statistically significant group difference reported by a cited study; the review does not define clinical impairment.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not discussed for the cited studies.

analysis.effect_sizes: Second-hand only. From meta-analyses as summarized: Laws and Kokkalis (2007), 26 studies, short-term memory d -0.63, long-term memory -0.87, verbal memory -1.00, visual memory -0.27 (§3.2, 2nd paragraph, p. 5); Rogers et al. (2009), deficits on six memory measures against both non-using and polydrug-using controls but not on IQ (§3.5, p. 7). From imaging as summarized: SERT -19% to -46% across the cortex and -21% in the hippocampus in 49 people who used ecstasy against 50 controls (Kish et al., 2010; p. 4). No intervals, heterogeneity statistics or publication-bias assessments are given.
analysis.selective_reporting: Unsystematic selection guided by the core hypothesis; critiques not cited (see sample.selection_effects).

interpretation_gap.results_show: As summarized: lower average scores on memory and complex tasks in people abstinent from ecstasy in many but not all cross-sectional studies, normal performance on most simple tasks, small declines on some memory tests in two prospective cohorts with low use, lower SERT binding in most imaging studies, and associations of several measures with lifetime use. Persistence after stopping is uncertain on the author's own account.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions present the differences as functional deficits caused by serotonergic neurotoxicity, for example that MDMA-induced serotonergic neurotoxicity can impair memory (§6.2, 3rd paragraph, p. 15) and that the original model has been confirmed (§6.2, 1st paragraph, p. 14), and treat abstinent people who use ecstasy as having documented neurotoxicity (§5.3, p. 14). The practical-implications passage extends the laboratory differences to impairment in almost every occupation (§6.2, 5th paragraph, p. 15) without any study of occupational outcomes. Causal verbs are drawn from cross-sectional data, and the same section concedes that whether the problems endure cannot be answered on current evidence (§6.2, 6th paragraph, p. 15).

timeline.event: Prospective cohort of 188 people who had not used ecstasy, with incident use associated with a decline in verbal memory.
Critical review of executive working memory, summarized in this review (§3.4).
Study of people who used ecstasy with minimal exposure to other drugs, summarized in this review (§3.5).
The same author's letter on Halpern et al. (2011), which describes that study differently from this review.
Systematic review and meta-analysis of neurocognition after sustained abstinence (online 2025), read by the other reader of this batch.

replication.where_it_stands: The fullest statement in this batch of the view that recreational ecstasy causes serotonergic neurotoxicity with functional consequences. Its descriptions of individual studies should be checked against the primary papers before they are cited.

funding.funder: Not reported. The acknowledgements state only that the article was written during a sabbatical at the Centre for Human Psychopharmacology, Swinburne University, Melbourne (p. 15).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the in-press proof.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychology, Swansea University, UK. The explanatory model and roughly 30 of the cited studies are the author's own or co-authored; recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: Large prospective cohorts that measure memory and SERT binding before first use and repeatedly afterwards, with hair-verified use, a retested non-using control group and follow-up after people stop, analysed with pre-specified outcomes; and studies that relate within-person change in SERT binding to within-person change in memory.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; selection guided by the stated hypothesis.
No appraisal; several descriptions are wrong when checked (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The model is the author's, and roughly 30 references are his own or co-authored.
The model is said to be confirmed, causal verbs are used for cross-sectional findings, and occupational impairment is asserted without data.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against serotonergic neurotoxicity and functional deficits
domains.note: Critiques of the literature are not cited; null and premorbid findings are reported but treated as compatible with the model.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used. The review is a useful map of the literature reporting deficits and of the author's model, and may be cited for those. Its figures are second-hand, several are misreported, and claims should cite the primary studies or systematic reviews instead; any claim resting only on this review stays at draft.

key_findings.finding: Abstract: the review states that declarative memory, prospective memory and higher cognitive skills are often impaired in people abstinent from ecstasy, that deficits are often related to lifetime dose (slight in light use, more pronounced in heavy use), and that abstinent people who use ecstasy can show deficits in a wide range of functions with a serotonergic component.

Scope: the author describes the empirical literature as still fairly limited, with neurocognition the only area extensively studied, and states the review's core hypothesis that abstinent people who use ecstasy will show deficits in functions modulated by serotonin.

Animal findings and their interpretation: serotonergic neurotoxicity after MDMA is described as robust in many laboratory species since the mid-1980s, with distal loss of serotonin axon terminals the predominant hypothesis; the review reports an alternative reading, neuroadaptive change without terminal loss, and a call for a clearer definition of neurotoxicity (Biezonski and Meyer, 2011), who nonetheless conclude that MDMA can be called neurotoxic in the sense of causing serotonergic dysfunction.

Human imaging: the first studies, in the late 1990s, found reduced serotonergic markers in people abstinent from ecstasy compared with non-using controls; the evidence was critically reviewed in the mid-2000s for the specificity of the markers; not every study found deficits, a variation attributed to lifetime dose, duration of abstinence, radioligand, brain region, sex, polydrug use and sample size; reviews concluded that lower SERT density is the most robust finding.

Kish et al. (2010), as summarized: 49 people with moderate ecstasy use against 50 non-using controls; SERT binding lower in every cortical region (-19% to -46%) and in the hippocampus (-21%), related to the extent of use, after control for many confounds (recent use checked by hair analysis; other drugs, sex, gene polymorphism and chronic tolerance monitored). Studies of heavier use also found subcortical reductions.

Other drugs: the author argues that SERT changes are probably due to MDMA rather than other drugs, citing a post-mortem case of one person who used ecstasy (and also cocaine and heroin) with striatal serotonin 60% to 77% lower and normal dopamine (Kish et al., 2000), and a PET study in which a group preferring MDMA had SERT binding lower by 56% in the neocortex, 19% in the pallidostriatum and 32% in the amygdala, correlated with lifetime MDMA use, while a group preferring hallucinogens showed no change (Erritzoe et al., 2011).
key_findings.note: The review's argument that the transporter changes are due to MDMA rather than other drugs rests partly on a theoretical claim, that most other recreational drugs do not have strong serotonergic effects (proof lines 211-217), and partly on the single post-mortem case and the hallucinogen comparison described here. No analysis is presented.

key_findings.finding: Two imaging studies summarized with null or mixed results: an fMRI study of cortical excitability found no significant group difference in any brain region, with lifetime use associated with greater activation in some regions (Bauernfeind et al., 2011); in a prospective imaging study of 188 people who had not used ecstasy, the 59 who had used it by follow-up at 17 months (mean 6.0 tablets, median 2.0) did not differ from 56 controls in SERT, which the author attributes to the very low use, but differed on blood-volume and diffusion measures (de Win et al., 2008).
key_findings.note: The de Win et al. (2008) cohort appears to be the same 188-person Netherlands XTC Toxicity cohort as Schilt et al. (2007) (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Cerebrospinal fluid: one study is summarized as finding that more use per month went with lower immediate verbal and delayed visual memory, and that lower CSF 5-HIAA went with poorer memory (Bolla et al., 1998). The review does not discuss CSF 5-HIAA group differences otherwise.

Memory meta-analyses as summarized: Laws and Kokkalis (2007), 26 studies with calculable effect sizes: short-term memory d -0.63, long-term memory -0.87, verbal memory -1.00, visual memory -0.27; Rogers et al. (2009), over 100 studies: deficits significant against both non-using and polydrug-using controls, with strength varying by task; Nulsen et al. (2010): poorer performance in all memory domains, with drug-naive or polydrug-using controls.
key_findings.note: Second-hand; none of the meta-analyses was read; no intervals or heterogeneity given. Rogers et al. (2009) is a Health Technology Assessment systematic review of observational evidence (Health Technology Assessment 13(6), 1-315), not a primary study; cite that synthesis rather than this review's description of it.

key_findings.finding: Small prospective series as summarized: 15 people tested a year apart, during which their lifetime use rose from an average of 19 to 55 occasions, declined on Rivermead paragraph recall but not on two WAIS subtests (Zakzanis and Young, 2001); at 2 years, the 8 who had stopped were unchanged or improved and the 7 who continued were unchanged or worse, with the Rivermead overall memory score rising from 19.9 to 22.9 in those who stopped and falling from 17.4 to 9.2 in those who continued (Zakzanis and Campbell, 2006).
key_findings.note: No retested control group; editors' calculation: the fall in the continuing group is 47%, not over 50% as the review says.

key_findings.finding: Prospective cohorts as summarized: of 149 people almost naive to ecstasy at baseline, 23 who had used a mean of 13.5 tablets over the following year were compared with 43 cannabis-using controls; most tasks did not differ, but figural visual recognition (immediate and delayed) was poorer (Wagner et al., 2013). Of 188 people who had not used ecstasy, 58 who then used an average of 3.2 tablets were compared with 60 who did not; there were no baseline differences, and at retest the ecstasy group was worse on immediate and delayed verbal recall and verbal recognition (Schilt et al., 2007).
key_findings.note: The retest interval for Schilt et al. is misreported (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Working memory: a review of 33 studies (Murphy et al., 2009) is summarized as finding performance normal on most working-memory tasks, executive shifting and most inhibition tasks unaffected, and deficits most apparent on tasks requiring updating of verbal information and on visuospatial tasks needing processing beyond storage.

Lifetime-use gradient as summarized: in one study, Tower of London planning time per solution was 6.5 s in polydrug-using controls, 8.9 s with low, 9.8 s with medium and 15.3 s with high lifetime ecstasy use, and correct answers on a spatial memory task fell with lifetime use (Fox et al., 2001).

Other drugs: the author states that deficits generally remain after control for polydrug use; in Rogers et al. (2009) people who used ecstasy showed deficits on all six memory measures (RAVLT immediate and delayed, RBMT immediate and delayed prose recall, digit span forwards and backwards) against both non-using and polydrug-using controls, IQ was not lower than in polydrug-using controls, and deficits were generally strongest against non-using controls.
key_findings.note: Rogers et al. (2009) is a Health Technology Assessment systematic review of observational evidence (Health Technology Assessment 13(6), 1-315), not a primary study; cite that synthesis rather than this review's description of it.

key_findings.finding: Studies with minimal other drug use as summarized: in Halpern et al. (2004) the light-use subgroup did not differ from non-using controls, while the heavy-use subgroup was poorer on Wisconsin card sorting, Stroop interference and the Revised Strategy Application test; in Yip and Lee (2005), who excluded people with illicit polydrug histories, basic working memory was normal and verbal memory, non-verbal memory and complex attention were poorer; in Halpern et al. (2011) the overall group had few deficits, and the heavier subgroup is said to have been impaired on spatial span forwards, digit span backwards, the strategy test and the non-dominant-hand pegboard.
key_findings.note: The description of Halpern et al. (2011) is partly wrong (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Summary of the cognitive evidence: many simple cognitive skills are not impaired, and even on tasks that often show deficits they are not universally found; in Rogers et al. (2009) individual studies of digit span and of verbal immediate recall were a mixture of significant and non-significant results, with significant pooled estimates; the author suggests sample size, participant selection and control of error variance as reasons.

Pre-existing psychiatric differences as summarized: in a prospective survey of 2462 young people aged 14-24 at baseline and reassessed 4 years later, people who had used ecstasy or amphetamines had higher rates of almost all DSM-IV disorders, which in most cases preceded the drug use (Lieb et al., 2002); childhood anxiety and depression predicted later ecstasy use in 1580 Dutch young people (Huizink et al., 2006) but not in 2143 Australian young people (odds ratio 1.0; Alati et al., 2007).

Pregnancy (§3.10): the review summarizes a prospective cohort of 28 women who used ecstasy (group mean 25 tablets) around conception and in the first trimester, against 68 women who used other psychoactive drugs in pregnancy; it reports lower scores on the Bayley Psychomotor Developmental Index and other psychomotor ratings at 4 months, a relation with the amount used, continuing differences at 12 and 24 months in the children of the women who had used most, and no differences in other child behavioural or psychological ratings (Singer et al., 2012a, 2012b, 2013). It also cites a report of more congenital abnormalities, mainly cardiac and musculo-skeletal, among women who had used ecstasy in pregnancy (McElhatton et al., 1999).
key_findings.note: Second-hand: none of these studies was read, the comparison group also used other drugs, and the review gives no intervals.

key_findings.finding: SERT and cognition: two PET studies (described as fMRI) are summarized as finding SERT reductions and associations with cognition: memory performance associated with SERT binding in dorsolateral prefrontal, orbitofrontal and parietal cortex (McCann et al., 2008), and poorer short-term memory, mental flexibility and speed associated with SERT loss in the insula and hippocampus, with simple tasks unimpaired and complex tasks impaired (Kish et al., 2010).
key_findings.note: The direction of the McCann et al. association is worded inconsistently (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Current against former use as summarized: in a PET study, people who had stopped using ecstasy showed some selective memory deficits against controls while people currently using did not, whereas on imaging the current group differed from polydrug-using controls and the former group did not (Thomasius et al., 2003).

An electrophysiology study found higher loudness dependence of auditory evoked potentials in people abstinent from ecstasy, related to cumulative use; its authors noted that prospective studies were still needed because premorbid differences between groups might explain the cross-sectional findings (Daumann et al., 2006, as summarized).

Tolerance and stopping (§5.2): the review states that people who use ecstasy typically stop on their own after a few years, that in a survey of 430 people the most frequently reported long-term effect was tolerance, with 90% reporting a decline in the drug's effect with repeated use (Verheyden et al., 2003a), and that a follow-up study of reasons for stopping reported the same decline (Verheyden et al., 2003b). The author's hypothesis is that loss of serotonin function reduces the subjective effect, which in turn leads to heavier patterns of use; he presents this as his own model, not as a tested finding.
key_findings.locator: §5.2 Quitting Ecstasy/MDMA and serotonergic neurotoxicity, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (proof lines 1267-1309)
key_findings.note: Second-hand: the surveys were not read. Recorded because tolerance is a standard question on every monograph (METHODS §8, section 5) and no other source in this batch covers it.

key_findings.finding: Early proposals: the review reports that earlier authors noted that premorbid factors should be considered (Gerra et al.) and that serotonergic effects might be modulated by predisposition (Schifano, 2000), and quotes a 2002 review stating that, because of methodological problems, no conclusions could yet be established on ecstasy toxicity in the human brain (Kish et al., 2002). The next section states that recent findings have confirmed the original model.

Model: in many aspects of behaviour people abstinent from ecstasy are not impaired; most basic cognitive, visual and psychomotor skills remain intact, the degree of loss is often subtle, and the overall memory system is described as retained while serotonergic neurotoxicity is said to impair memory.

Practical implications: the author argues that most occupations need memory, planning and organization and are therefore likely to be impaired, giving examples of occupations and concluding that it is difficult to think of any occupational activity that would not be impaired; no study of occupational outcomes is cited.

Persistence: a case study is summarized of one man whose problems had not resolved after 7 years of abstinence (Soar et al., 2004); the author states that whether the problems endure over time cannot be answered on current evidence, that there are some indications that they do (Morgan et al., 2002) but the data are very limited, and that prospective studies with imaging and comprehensive functional measures are needed.

reporting_issues.issue: Two PET studies of SERT (McCann et al., 2008; Kish et al., 2010; their PET methods are named in their titles in the review's own reference list) are called fMRI studies, in Table 4 and in §4.1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Mislabelled method; fMRI cannot measure SERT. Cite the studies by their own methods.

reporting_issues.issue: Halpern et al. (2011) is misdescribed: the review says the heavier-use subgroup was impaired on spatial span forwards and digit span backwards, but in Halpern et al.'s Table 3 neither differs in that subgroup (p=0.18 and 0.15); spatial span forwards differed in the overall group (p=0.04) and the moderate subgroup (p=0.04), and digits backwards only in the overall group (p=0.05) (checked by this reader, PMC HTML, Tables 2-3). The author's own 2011 letter gives the correct pattern. The citation Halpern et al. (2011a,b) also points to a 2011b reference that is a different study of emergency-department morbidity by other authors named Halpern (reference list, p. 16).
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's account of the minimal-polydrug study overstates a dose gradient; claims must cite Halpern et al.'s tables.

reporting_issues.issue: The Schilt et al. (2007) cohort is said to have been retested 18-36 months later; Schilt et al. report a mean retest interval of 11.1 months (SD 6.2) in the ecstasy group and 19.1 months (SD 7.5) in controls (Schilt et al. PDF, p. 731). The review also omits that study's statement that the scores of the people who started using stayed within the normal range (its abstract, p. 728), and presents de Win et al. (2008) as a separate prospective study, although Schilt et al. describe their study as part of the Netherlands XTC Toxicity study with a baseline sample of 188 (pp. 728-729), the same study name and number the review gives for de Win et al., so the two appear to report one cohort; that cohort's mean age was 22 years (Schilt et al., p. 728), not teenagers as the review says.
reporting_issues.consequence: The prospective evidence presented as two studies appears to be one cohort, with unequal retest intervals that the review does not mention; claims should rest on Schilt et al. directly.

reporting_issues.issue: The decline in the 7 continuing participants of Zakzanis and Campbell (2006), from 17.4 to 9.2, is 47% (editors' calculation), described as over 50% on p. 6 and as 50% lower than baseline on p. 15; there was no retested control group, and the 8 who stopped improved from 19.9 to 22.9, which may include practice effects.
reporting_issues.consequence: Small overstatement of an uncontrolled change in seven people.

reporting_issues.issue: The direction of the SERT-memory association is worded inconsistently: §4.1 says memory performance was inversely associated with SERT binding (which, read literally, means lower binding with better memory), while Table 4 says lower SERT went with poorer memory and the same paragraph calls it a positive association between deficits and serotonergic reductions.
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction must be taken from McCann et al. (2008) itself.

reporting_issues.issue: A survey of 329 people is summarized with the majority (n=136, 46%) changing their behaviour alone; 136 is 41% of 329, and 46% is not a majority (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor and outside the claims of this batch; another sign that the review's figures need checking at source.

reporting_issues.issue: The PDF is the uncorrected in-press proof, with open author queries (Q1-Q3) and a list of uncited references (p. 15); whether the printed article (pp. 1466-1484) corrected any of these errors was not checked.
reporting_issues.consequence: Anchors cite the proof's page numbers; the editor should check the printed version before publication.

reporting_issues.issue: The prospective cohort summarized at p. 6 as Wagner et al. (2013) has no entry in the proof's reference list: the only occurrences of that surname are co-authorships of other cited papers (Bosch et al., 2013; Mithoefer et al., 2011; Quednow et al., 2004). A reader cannot identify one of the two prospective cohorts the review relies on.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's second prospective cohort cannot be traced from this source; claims must not describe it as a second cohort on this basis (see cl_mdma_prospective). Whether the printed article supplies the entry was not checked.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1-19 of the in-press proof (PDFs/MDMA/Parrott_2013_NeurotoxicityFunctionalDeficits.pdf): all pages read, pp. 5-8 rendered and Tables 1-4 checked; the printed article is pp. 1466-1484 (not checked). Descriptions of Halpern et al. (2011) were checked against its PMC full text (PMC3053129), and of Schilt et al. (2007) against its PDF in this batch.
